strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized; the Bayesian framing with explicit/implicit evidence fusion, discounting (λ), and Thompson sampling forms a coherent and extensible framework for online task selection in RFT.

Comprehensive experimental coverage: two model scales (1.5B/7B), three domains (math/code/logic), extensive ablations over ρ and λ, an analysis of posterior sampling, wall-clock overhead analysis (≤0.2%), and a large appendix with formal metric definitions and hyperparameter tables.

Honest and transparent discussion of limitations (linear interpolation assumption, distributional shift in µt, fixed λ/ρ, reference model sensitivity), and clean proofs of the Beta-family closure and effective-sample-size bounds.
The motivation for fusing two complementary evidence sources (cold-start benefit of implicit evidence, long-term accuracy of explicit evidence) is empirically well-supported and instructive.
Negligible computational overhead is a genuine practical advantage over oversampling-based alternatives.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in the core machinery: the method is essentially a discounted Beta-Bernoulli bandit with Thompson sampling (standard), plus a very simple linear interpolation between two pre-computed reference model success rates. The main contribution is a combination and systematization of existing ideas (MoPPS, DOTS) rather than a new technique.

Baselines are only within-framework 'proxies' (BOTS-MoPPS, BOTS-DOTS) rather than faithful reimplementations of the published methods being compared against; the Offline baseline ranks tasks by external models rather than reproducing specific published curricula.

Empirical gains are modest and inconsistent: BSF improvements are often ~1-8%, many cells show second-best rather than best results (e.g., Logic-1.5B where Offline's BSF dominates), and downstream performance often converges across methods (notably Code-7B and Logic-7B), which weakens the significance claim.

No error bars, seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported for expensive RFT runs; TTB/BSF are ratios computed on single training trajectories, and small evaluation sets (AIME24: 30 problems, ARC-AGI) make these ratios highly noise-sensitive.

Potential evaluation circularity: the recommended default setting (λ=0.1, ρ=0.1) is selected from ablations on the same benchmarks used for the headline comparison, so the 'recommended setting' may be tuned to the test tasks; ETR is also estimated from the same 16 rollouts used for training.

Key design choices lack ablation: no systematic study of reference model pairings (only Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct/Qwen3-32B), momentum coefficient γ, prior parameters, or batch composition; sensitivity of results to the target p*=0.5 is not examined.

The interpolation estimator's predictive quality degrades substantially for the 7B model late in training (ROC AUC → 0.5), and BOTS-DOTS performs nearly identically to full BOTS in several settings, raising questions about how much the explicit/implicit fusion actually contributes over the implicit-only proxy.
Generalization claims (non-binary rewards, exponential-family extension) remain theoretical-only, restricted to discussion in the appendix without experiments.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated and clearly written: it identifies a real and practical problem (adaptive task selection in LLM RFT) and articulates the tension between rollout cost and estimation accuracy in existing methods.

The Bayesian formulation is clean and self-consistent: the generalized Beta-Bernoulli update (Prop. 1), the effective-sample-size analysis (Prop. 2), and the λ/ρ interpretation as exploration–exploitation knobs are correct and help interpret the hyperparameters.

The evaluation is broad for the field: two model scales (1.5B, 7B), three domains (math, code, logic), multiple ablations (ρ, λ, posterior sampling), wall-clock overhead analysis (<0.2%), and informative fine-grained visualizations (task success-rate heatmaps) that explain the behavior of the method.
The proposed method has genuinely negligible computational overhead, which is a practical advantage over oversampling-based alternatives.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core components are largely re-combinations of existing ideas: explicit-evidence bandit selection (MoPPS, Qu et al. 2025), implicit inter-task evidence (DOTS, Sun et al. 2025), and standard Thompson sampling. The claimed unification amounts to two extra mixing coefficients (λ, ρ) in a Beta update. The 'ultra-light interpolation plug-in' is a one-line linear interpolation between pre-computed success rates of two reference models — an engineering heuristic rather than a methodological contribution.

The empirical gains are modest and inconsistent. Headline numbers are thin: e.g., final BSF ≈ 1.05 on math (1.5B), and the paper's own tables show BOTS winning only 6–8 of 18 metrics against its own ablations, with BOTS-DOTS often matching or exceeding BOTS (Code, and nearly identical on Math-7B). No statistical significance testing, and results appear to come from single training runs without seed variance, despite TTB/BSF being highly sensitive to curve noise.

The baselines are proxies rather than faithful reimplementations: 'BOTS-MoPPS' and 'BOTS-DOTS' are special cases of the authors' own framework (with borrowed hyperparameters), not the original systems. Direct comparisons against published implementations of the strongest competitors are missing.

Method validity depends on fragile assumptions: the interpolation requires weak/strong reference models that bracket the training trajectory (admitted in Appendix E.3), and the estimator's Pearson correlation hovers around only ~0.5, degrading to ROC AUC ≈ 0.5 for the 7B model in later training. No systematic ablation of reference model choice is provided.

The theoretical results are elementary: Prop. 1 is an algebraic closure check of Beta-conjugacy, and Prop. 2 is a straightforward bound on a linear recurrence; neither addresses the actual difficulty of the problem (regret under non-stationarity, or the effect of biased implicit evidence on selection).
Scope is narrow: only binary rewards, only Qwen models on one dataset (GURU). The footnoted code release link is empty ('Our code is released at'), undermining reproducibility claims.

The hyperparameter discussion (small positive ρ, moderate λ best) is post-hoc tuning narrative rather than a principled selection rule; the authors themselves defer adaptive schemes to future work, weakening the 'principled framework' claim.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated and clearly written: the online task selection problem for LLM RFT is framed as non-stationary Bayesian inference, and the decomposition into explicit (direct rollout) vs. implicit (interpolated) evidence is intuitive and well-argued.

The core technical contribution is cleanly presented: a generalized-Bayes update (Eq. 1, Prop. 1) that provably preserves Beta conjugacy, plus an analysis (Prop. 2) of how the hyperparameters λ and ρ control the effective sample size and hence the exploration–exploitation balance. The proofs in Appendix D are correct and the exponential-family generalization (Appendix E.4.1) is a nice extensibility argument.

The interpolation-based implicit-evidence plug-in is genuinely lightweight: no extra rollouts, ≤0.2% wall-clock overhead (Appendix F.1), and relies on pre-computed reference-model success rates that are already routinely computed in RL dataset curation.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: ablations over both ρ and λ with clear, well-supported takeaways; comparisons at two model scales (1.5B, 7B) and three domains (math, code, logic); overhead breakdowns; qualitative validation of the interpolator (Pearson/ROC-AUC trajectories); and heatmap analyses of selected-task difficulty dynamics that directly support the mechanism's claimed behavior.

The ablation design that reduces the framework to MoPPS-like (λ=0, ρ=0) and DOTS-like (λ=1, ρ=1) settings is a fair and transparent way to isolate the contribution of evidence fusion, and the honest reporting that BOTS-DOTS can be competitive (e.g., on code) increases credibility.
Reproducibility is supported by extensive hyperparameter tables, dataset details, code release, and formal metric definitions (TTB, BSF).
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than high: Beta-Bernoulli posteriors with discounting, Thompson sampling, and difficulty-targeted bandit selection are all established tools; the main advance is their combination with a simple linear interpolation estimator. The 'first unified framework' claim is positioning rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The gains are real but modest: best-so-far improvements of ~3–8% (BSF ≈ 1.03–1.08) and step-efficiency gains that are not uniform across domains. With no error bars, seed variance, or statistical significance tests on the TTB/BSF metrics (which are ratios and can be sensitive to noise on small benchmarks like AIME24), some of the 'first-place/second-place counts' analysis may overstate the reliability of the differences.

Comparison with prior work relies on within-framework proxies (re-implemented MoPPS/DOTS configurations) rather than the original methods, including their additional components (e.g., DOTS's rollout replay). The paper is transparent about this, but it means the headline claim of superiority over existing approaches is only indirectly supported. Notably absent is any comparison against oversampling-based filtering baselines (e.g., DAPO-style dynamic sampling), which are cited as a major category of prior work.

Several design choices are under-justified: the target difficulty p* = 0.5 is taken from prior work without ablation; the reference-model pair (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct / Qwen3-32B) is chosen heuristically and the authors themselves acknowledge no systematic ablation; and the linear interpolation assumption's bias (µ estimated on adaptively selected, non-uniform batches) is discussed but not corrected.

Scope limitations are acknowledged but not addressed: binary rewards only, a single RL algorithm (GRPO), fixed λ/ρ despite the authors' own finding that different values suit different training stages, and unclear behavior when the training model outgrows the strong reference model (the 7B results already show the implicit estimator degrading, ROC-AUC → 0.5).

The evaluation metric design (TTB/BSF relative to a random baseline) makes cross-paper comparison difficult, and the 'counts of first-place finishes out of 18 metrics' framing can be misleading when differences are small.
